newsitem.title: GERMANY: Allies observe Cold War history in Berlin.
newsitem.headline: Allies observe Cold War history in Berlin.

text.p: Two years after the last Western Allied soldiers left Berlin, a group of French, British and American representatives returned on Thursday to join the Germans in preserving Cold War history.

The Allies Museum, a collection of memorabilia from the 49 years of Western military presence in Berlin, was turned over to a council of Allied and German diplomats and historians by the German Historical Museum that organised the exhibit.

Located in the former U.S. army cinema called "Outpost Theater", the museum's permanent collection is a tribute to the tenuous half-century of Cold War and the Allies' role in protecting West Berlin from a feared Soviet invasion.
"This museum marks the course of our relationship with the Allies from occupiers to protectors to partners to, finally, friends," said Helmut Trotnow, director of the museum's managing council.
The official opening of the completed museum is planned for June 1998 to mark the 50th anniversary of the Berlin blockade and the airlift.

There were about 12,000 troops from the Western Allies stationed throughout the Cold War in West Berlin, an island of democracy surrounded by communist East Germany and more than 338,000 Soviet soldiers.
The new directors opened a temporary exhibit at the museum called "Every object tells a story", which features personal mementos, art work and weapons of the Western Allies.
An east Berliner donated a British Airways flight ticket to Hamburg dated August 14, 1961, one day before the Berlin Wall was erected and travel from east to west was restricted.
"W. Stoermer" kept the ticket until the Wall finally fell in 1989, when the airline allowed him to trade it in for a free flight anywhere in the country.

Much of the museum's permanent collection recalls the 1948/49 airlift to West Berlin, after the Soviets cut off road and rail access to the enclave in an ultimately failed attempt to force out the Western Allies.
The Allies flew in more than 500 planeloads of supplies every day for 10 months to the isolated city.

"We now enjoy a much better relationship with Russia," said Trotnow. "But this is not a harmonious history. We didn't often work together with the Russians and we were often harshly in opposition to each other."
Neither the Russians nor the Allied troops fired a single shot in anger during the Berlin occupation, but the museum displays relics from the strained half-century of German cohabitation.

One of the five U.S. M48A2 tanks that faced off a few metres (yards) away from 10 Soviet tanks in a tense Cold War stand-off in 1961 was donated to the museum by the Western allies in 1994 but will remain in storage until 1998.
The Russians have their own museum in east Berlin, documenting their presence in the Soviet sector after the Nazi defeat in World War Two.
